title: The four riders (Revelation 6)
hook: conquest, war, famine and death ride out

segments.voice: Yesterday, the slain Lamb: John heard lion, looked, and saw a lamb. Your line was the lamb is the lion. Where did you try the gentle way? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

The Lamb takes the scroll and breaks the first seal. There's a sound like thunder, and one of the living creatures says, "Come and see." A white horse comes out, its rider holding a bow, wearing a crown, going out "conquering, and to conquer." Second seal: a red horse, and its rider is given power "to take peace from the earth." Third: a black horse, its rider holding a pair of scales. Fourth: a pale horse, "and his name that sat on him was Death." Four riders, out into the world. Readers have named them conquest, war, famine and death. But a quieter moment in this chapter comes after the horses have gone.

First, the riders themselves. The red one is given a great sword, "that they should kill one another." The black one carries scales, and a voice calls out prices: "A measure of wheat for a penny, and three measures of barley for a penny; and see thou hurt not the oil and the wine." Grain is dear, while the oil and the wine are spared. The pale one is Death, "and Hell followed with him." The white rider is argued over. Some readers hear plain conquest. Others hear Christ, because a rider on a white horse returns later in the book. The text doesn't settle it here. Second, who opens the seals: the Lamb. Readers differ on what that means. Some see judgment. Others see Revelation unveiling what the world already does, and showing that even Death and Hell have limits: power was given them "over the fourth part of the earth." Not over all of it. Third, the fifth seal. No horse this time. John sees, under the altar, the souls of those killed for the word of God, and they cry out: "How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?" How long. It's the question of the Psalms: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?" Scripture lets people ask God that, out loud, in heaven itself. Fourth, the answer. It isn't an explanation. "White robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season." A robe, and rest, and a question left open for now.

Here's the practice: hold places of war and hunger. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place you know of where people are at war, or going hungry. Don't flood yourself with pictures; one is enough. Hold it gently, the way you'd hold someone's hand in a hospital. If you pray, you can name that place before God, or borrow the words from under the altar: how long, O Lord. If you don't pray, simply keep it in your attention for a few slow breaths, and let it matter to you. Then, if you can, bring a second place to mind. The bell holds the time.
The four riders. Conquest, war, famine and death, released as the Lamb opens the seals, and then a question from under the altar: how long?
Your line: how long? Today, when the news shows you a place at war or going hungry, stop for one breath and hold it, instead of scrolling past. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Christians pray for places suffering war and famine in their own prayers and in the prayers of the people during services, and some churches pray in lament using the Psalms' cry of 'how long'.

fork.setup: you're under the altar with those killed for the word of God. the riders have gone out. you've waited. what do you do?
options: stay silent; questions aren't allowed in heaven.
cry out: how long, O Lord?
fork.reveal: they cry, "How long, O Lord, holy and true?" and they aren't silenced: they're given white robes and told to rest a little season.

original.note: Greek: pale, with a greenish tinge. the color of the fourth horse in Revelation 6:8.

trapdoor: what you thought: the four horsemen are an end-of-the-world movie.
what it means: four riders released as the Lamb opens the seals, with limits on their power, and then martyrs asking God, how long?
what a scholar hears: some read the white rider as Christ (cf. Revelation 19:11), others as conquest; the cry of 6:10 echoes the lament of Psalm 13.
recall: the first and last Greek letters

notes: Famine is read from the prices of 6:6 ('grain is dear'); no wage figure is given by design.
The white rider: two readings named (conquest; Christ, cf. 19:11), unranked. Confirm.
Two readings of the Lamb opening the seals (judgment; unveiling what the world already does, with limits) named without ranking. Confirm.
The hook calls the fifth seal 'a quieter moment in this chapter' (no horse, a question). Confirm.
Original: χλωρός glossed 'pale, with a greenish tinge'. Confirm.
Practice deliberately names no current war or famine.
Editor pass: the 'fourth part of the earth' limit is given to Death and Hell (6:8), not to all four riders; review says John 'looked', matching day 1298.
